questions.problem: If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ is a sample of size $n=20$ drawn from a population with mean $\mu =0.7$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.1,$ calculate the value of $\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}].$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}.
$$

Since the population variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.1$ and the sample size $n=20,$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}] & =\frac{0.1}{20} \\  & =0.005.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{8}$ is a sample of size $n=8$ drawn from a population with mean $\mu =30$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=16,$ calculate the standard error of $\overset{―}{X}.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Since the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=16$ and the sample size is $n=8,$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}] & =\frac{16}{8} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{2}≈1.41.
$$

questions.problem: A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ of four bills is drawn from a population. The population has bills of two different denominations, $$5$ and $$10,$ distributed in the ratio $3:2.$ Calculate the standard error of $\overset{―}{X}.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the bills in the population have denominations $$5$ and $$10,$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:2.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+2=5$ bills only with the following denominations:

$$
$5,\,$5,\,$5,\,$10\,$10.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot 5+2\cdot 10) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(15+20) \\  & =\frac{35}{5} \\  & =$7,\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot {5}^{2}+2\cdot {10}^{2})-{7}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(275)-49 \\  & =55-49 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size is $n=4,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{6}{4}=1.5.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{1.5}≈$1.22.
$$

questions.problem: If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with mean $\mu =5$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=4,$  determine the smallest sample size required so that the standard error of the mean is less than $0.02.$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}
$$

Since the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{4}=2,$ we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $0.02.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}} & <0.02 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{2}{0.02} \\ \sqrt{n} & >100 \\ n & >{100}^{2} \\ n & >10\,000.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest sample size is $n=10\,001.$

questions.problem: A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ of $n$ coins is drawn from a population. The population has coins of two different denominations, $$1$ and $$0.50,$ distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Determine the smallest sample size required so that the standard error of the mean is less than $$0.02.$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the coins in the population have denominations $$1$ and $$0.50,$ and these are distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $1+4=5$ coins only with the following denominations:

$$
$1,\,$0.5,\,$0.5,\,$0.5,\,$0.5.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+4\cdot 0.5) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+2) \\  & =\frac{3}{5} \\  & =$0.6,\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({1}^{2}+4\cdot {0.5}^{2})-{0.6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2)-0.36 \\  & =0.4-0.36 \\  & =0.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.04}=0.2,$ and we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{0.2}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $$0.02.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.2}{\sqrt{n}} & <0.02 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{0.2}{0.02} \\ \sqrt{n} & >10 \\ n & >{10}^{2} \\ n & >100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest sample size is $n=101.$
